tagline: Orchards and an old sugar shack along Londonderry’s town roads
intro: The Apple Way links orchards, old schoolhouses and farm sites along Londonderry’s roads. Visit NH presents it as a ten-mile agricultural tour and suggests allowing an hour or a whole day. The drive begins on Gilcreast Road and ends on Mammoth Road, with farms and former community buildings along the way. Late summer through fall is the prime apple-picking season.

At Moose Hill, John Mack founded a farm in 1732 after emigrating from Londonderry, Ireland. His family began concentrating on apples in the nineteenth century. Londonderry has since purchased conservation easements to preserve farm green space, including orchard land on Pillsbury Road.

Begin on Gilcreast Road by the town offices, passing Dutton Farm before turning east onto Pillsbury Road. Continue to High Range Road, with Jackson Hall and Sunnycrest Farm, then Elwood Road and Adams Road. The final stretch on Mammoth Road passes School House #2, Mack’s Orchards and Lions Hall, formerly Reverend William Morrison’s Meeting House. The Methodist Church, Grange #44 and Town Common also stand along Mammoth Road.

moments.title: Dutton Farm
moments.text: Behind Dutton Farm’s barn stands an old sugar shack. The farm was Londonderry’s first maple-syrup producer, and its sugar maples are tapped each spring. It lies on Gilcreast Road near the beginning of the Apple Way.
moments.notice: The old sugar shack stands behind the barn.

moments.title: High Range Road
moments.text: Jackson Hall began as Bell Tavern, giving High Range Road a connection to an earlier roadside use. The road also provides access to Sunnycrest Farm, with pick-your-own apples, strawberries and blueberries. Lithia Springs lies near the junction with NH 102.

moments.title: Mack's Orchards, Mammoth Road
moments.text: Mack’s Apples, also known as Moose Hill Orchards, began as John Mack’s farm in 1732. The family turned its attention toward growing apples in the nineteenth century, then ended wholesale operations in the early 2000s. Eight generations of Mack ownership ended with the farm’s sale to MHO Acquisitions LLC in 2021. The farm operates on approximately 400 acres, with 100 devoted to apples. Town conservation easements preserve green space here, including a 23-acre orchard parcel on Pillsbury Road. Mammoth Road also passes School House #2 and the former meeting house of Reverend William Morrison.
